stem: Name the components of the formed elements in the blood and mention one major function of each of them.
solution:
The formed elements of blood are **erythrocytes**, **leucocytes** and **platelets**; together they constitute nearly 45 per cent of the blood.

1. **Erythrocytes (red blood cells, RBC):** the most abundant cells of blood. They contain the iron containing protein **haemoglobin** and so **transport the respiratory gases**.
2. **Leucocytes (white blood cells, WBC):** nucleated, colourless cells concerned with the **defence of the body**.
   - **Neutrophils** and **monocytes** are phagocytic and destroy foreign organisms entering the body.
   - **Basophils** secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin and are involved in inflammatory reactions.
   - **Eosinophils** resist infections and are associated with allergic reactions.
   - **Lymphocytes** (B and T forms) are responsible for the immune responses of the body.
3. **Platelets (thrombocytes):** cell fragments produced from megakaryocytes. They release substances involved in the **coagulation (clotting) of blood**.
groundedIn: §15.1.2; Fig. 15.1 — erythrocytes, leucocytes and platelets are the formed elements (45 per cent); haemoglobin transports respiratory gases; functions of each WBC type; platelets release substances involved in clotting

stem: What is the importance of plasma proteins?
solution:
Plasma proteins make up 6-8 per cent of the plasma. The major ones are fibrinogen, globulins and albumins.

1. **Fibrinogen** is needed for the **clotting or coagulation of blood**; it is converted into fibrin threads by thrombin.
2. **Globulins** are primarily involved in the **defence mechanisms** of the body.
3. **Albumins** help in maintaining the **osmotic balance**.
groundedIn: §15.1.1; §15.1.4 — proteins are 6-8 per cent of plasma; fibrinogen for clotting, globulins in defence, albumins in osmotic balance; fibrinogen converted to fibrin by thrombin

stem: Why do we consider blood as a connective tissue?
solution:
Blood is considered a **special (fluid) connective tissue** because:

1. Like other connective tissues it consists of **cells scattered in an extracellular matrix**. In blood the matrix is a fluid, the **plasma**, and the cells are the **formed elements** (RBCs, WBCs and platelets).
2. It **connects all parts of the body**, transporting nutrients, \(\text{O}_2\) and other essential substances to the cells and carrying waste substances away from them.
3. Like other connective tissues, it is of **mesodermal origin**.
groundedIn: §15.1; §15.0 — blood is a special connective tissue consisting of a fluid matrix, plasma, and formed elements; transports essential substances to the cells and removes wastes (also stated in the chapter Summary); BEYOND CHAPTER: connective tissues consist of cells in an extracellular matrix; blood is of mesodermal origin

stem: What is the difference between lymph and blood?
solution:
Lymph is the tissue fluid collected by the lymphatic system. It resembles blood plasma but lacks the larger proteins and most of the formed elements.

| Basis | Lymph | Blood |
|---|---|---|
| Colour | Colourless | Red, due to haemoglobin in RBCs |
| Formed elements | No RBCs or platelets; contains specialised **lymphocytes** | Contains RBCs, WBCs and platelets (about 45 per cent of blood) |
| Proteins | Larger proteins are absent (left behind in the blood vessels) | Plasma contains 6-8 per cent proteins (fibrinogen, globulins, albumins) |
| Origin | Derived from blood: water and small soluble substances move out of the capillaries into the tissue spaces | RBCs are formed in the red bone marrow; platelets come from megakaryocytes of the bone marrow |
| Vessels | Flows in the **lymphatic system**, which drains it back into the major veins | Flows in a closed network of **blood vessels** pumped by the heart |
| Special function | Carries absorbed fats from the lacteals of intestinal villi; carries nutrients and hormones; lymphocytes give immune responses | Transports respiratory gases, nutrients and wastes; clots to prevent blood loss |
groundedIn: §15.2; §15.1.1; §15.1.2; §15.1.4; §15.3.1 — tissue fluid formed leaving larger proteins and most formed elements in vessels; lymph is colourless with specialised lymphocytes; fats absorbed through lymph in lacteals; lymph almost similar to blood except for protein content and formed elements (stated in the chapter Summary)

stem: What is meant by double circulation? What is its significance?
solution:
**Double circulation** is the pattern in which blood passes through the heart **twice** in one complete circuit of the body, through two separate pathways:

1. **Pulmonary circulation:** the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery to the lungs; the oxygenated blood returns by the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
2. **Systemic circulation:** the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta, which is carried by arteries, arterioles and capillaries to the tissues; deoxygenated blood is collected by venules, veins and vena cava and emptied into the right atrium.

It is seen in birds and mammals, which have a 4-chambered heart.

**Significance:**
1. The oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are pumped out by the two ventricles **without any mixing**, so the tissues receive fully oxygenated blood.
2. The systemic circulation efficiently supplies nutrients, \(\text{O}_2\) and other essential substances to the tissues and takes \(\text{CO}_2\) and other harmful substances away for elimination.
3. This efficient supply of oxygen supports the **high energy needs** of warm-blooded birds and mammals.
groundedIn: §15.4; §15.3; Fig. 15.4 — pulmonary and systemic circulation; in birds and mammals the ventricles pump blood out without any mixing, two separate pathways, hence double circulation; systemic circulation supplies nutrients and O2 and removes CO2; BEYOND CHAPTER: supports the high metabolic (energy) needs of warm-blooded birds and mammals

stem: Open and Closed system of circulation
solution:
| Basis | Open circulatory system | Closed circulatory system |
|---|---|---|
| Path of blood | Blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into **open spaces or body cavities** called **sinuses** | Blood pumped by the heart always circulates through a **closed network of blood vessels** |
| Contact with tissues | Blood in the sinuses bathes the tissues directly | Exchange with the cells takes place through the tissue fluid that leaves the capillaries |
| Regulation of flow | Flow cannot be precisely regulated | Flow can be **more precisely regulated**, so it is more advantageous |
| Examples | Arthropods and molluscs | Annelids and chordates |
groundedIn: §15.3; §15.2 — open system in arthropods and molluscs with sinuses; closed system in annelids and chordates, flow more precisely regulated; exchange between blood and cells occurs through interstitial fluid

stem: Describe the evolutionary change in the pattern of heart among the vertebrates.
solution:
All vertebrates possess a muscular chambered heart. The number of chambers increases from fishes to birds and mammals, and with it the separation of oxygenated from deoxygenated blood improves.

1. **Fishes: 2-chambered heart** with one atrium and one ventricle. The heart pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated by the gills and supplied to the body parts; deoxygenated blood returns to the heart. This is **single circulation**.
2. **Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles): 3-chambered heart** with two atria and a single ventricle. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the gills/lungs/skin and the right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body, but the two mix in the single ventricle, which pumps out mixed blood. This is **incomplete double circulation**.
3. **Crocodiles, birds and mammals: 4-chambered heart** with two atria and two ventricles. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood pass from the left and right atria to the ventricles of the same side and are pumped out **without mixing**. This is **double circulation**.
groundedIn: §15.3 — fishes 2-chambered, single circulation; amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles) 3-chambered with mixing, incomplete double circulation; crocodiles, birds and mammals 4-chambered; double circulation in birds and mammals

stem: Why do we call our heart myogenic?
solution:
Our heart is called **myogenic** because its normal activities are regulated **intrinsically**, i.e., auto regulated by specialised cardiac muscles, the **nodal tissue**.

1. The nodal musculature (SAN, AVN, AV bundle, purkinje fibres) is **autoexcitable**: it can generate action potentials without any external stimuli.
2. The heart beat is therefore initiated within the heart muscle itself. The neural centre in the medulla oblongata, through the autonomic nervous system, and the adrenal medullary hormones can only **moderate** the cardiac activity, not initiate it.
groundedIn: §15.5; §15.3.1 — heart is auto regulated by specialised muscles (nodal tissue), hence myogenic; nodal musculature generates action potentials without any external stimuli; ANS and adrenal medullary hormones moderate cardiac function

stem: Sino-atrial node is called the pacemaker of our heart. Why?
solution:
The **sino-atrial node (SAN)** is called the **pacemaker** because it **initiates and maintains the rhythmic contractile activity of the heart**.

1. The SAN is a patch of nodal tissue in the right upper corner of the right atrium.
2. All nodal tissue is autoexcitable, but the SAN generates the **maximum number of action potentials, 70-75 per minute**, more than any other part of the nodal system.
3. Each action potential from the SAN stimulates the atria to contract and is then conducted to the ventricles, so the SAN sets the pace of the heart beat (normally 70-75 beats per minute, average 72).
groundedIn: §15.3.1; §15.3.2 — SAN in the right upper corner of the right atrium; generates the maximum number of action potentials, 70-75 per minute, initiating and maintaining the rhythmic contractile activity, hence the pacemaker; SAN action potential stimulates atrial systole

stem: What is the significance of atrio-ventricular node and atrio-ventricular bundle in the functioning of heart?
solution:
The **atrio-ventricular node (AVN)** and the **atrio-ventricular bundle (AV bundle, bundle of His)** conduct the action potential from the atria to the ventricles, so that the ventricles contract after the atria.

1. The **AVN** is a mass of nodal tissue in the lower left corner of the right atrium, close to the atrio-ventricular septum. It picks up the action potential generated by the SAN after it has spread over the atria.
2. The **AV bundle** continues from the AVN, passes through the atrio-ventricular septa and divides on top of the inter-ventricular septum into a right and a left bundle. These give rise to the **purkinje fibres** throughout the ventricular musculature.
3. Through this pathway the action potential is transmitted through the **entire ventricular musculature**, causing the ventricles to contract (**ventricular systole**) in a coordinated way.
4. The impulse is slightly **delayed at the AVN**, which allows the atria to complete their contraction and empty blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.
groundedIn: §15.3.1; §15.3.2; Fig. 15.2 — AVN in the lower left corner of right atrium; AV bundle passes through AV septa, divides into right and left bundles giving purkinje fibres; action potential conducted to the ventricular side by AVN and AV bundle causing ventricular systole; BEYOND CHAPTER: the impulse is delayed at the AVN, letting the atria finish contracting before the ventricles contract

stem: Define a cardiac cycle and the cardiac output.
solution:
1. **Cardiac cycle:** the sequential events in the heart which are cyclically repeated, consisting of the **systole and diastole of both the atria and the ventricles**. The heart performs about 72 cardiac cycles per minute, so one cardiac cycle lasts **0.8 seconds**.
2. **Cardiac output:** the **volume of blood pumped out by each ventricle per minute**. It equals the **stroke volume** (about 70 mL per cycle) multiplied by the **heart rate** (beats per minute), and averages **5000 mL or 5 litres** in a healthy individual.
groundedIn: §15.3.2 — cardiac cycle consists of systole and diastole of both atria and ventricles; 72 per minute, duration 0.8 seconds; stroke volume about 70 mL; cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate, averages 5000 mL or 5 litres

solution:
During each cardiac cycle two prominent **heart sounds** are produced, which can be easily heard through a **stethoscope**.

1. **First heart sound (lub):** associated with the **closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves**. These valves close at the start of ventricular systole, when the rising ventricular pressure causes an attempted backflow of blood into the atria.
2. **Second heart sound (dub):** associated with the **closure of the semilunar valves**. These valves close at the start of ventricular diastole, when the falling ventricular pressure would otherwise let blood flow back from the pulmonary artery and aorta into the ventricles.
3. The heart sounds are of **clinical diagnostic significance**.
groundedIn: §15.3.2 — first heart sound (lub) with closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves; second (dub) with closure of semilunar valves; heard through a stethoscope; closure of valves at ventricular systole and diastole; of clinical diagnostic significance

stem: Draw a standard ECG and explain the different segments in it.
solution:
An **electrocardiogram (ECG)** is a graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle. A standard ECG is obtained with three leads (one to each wrist and to the left ankle).

**Diagram (labels a marker looks for):** a horizontal baseline drawn left to right with, in order: a small rounded upward wave labelled **P**; a small downward dip labelled **Q**; a tall, sharp upward spike labelled **R**; a downward dip below the baseline labelled **S** (Q, R and S together form the **QRS complex**); a broad, dome-shaped upward wave labelled **T**; then the baseline, with the next P-wave beginning. Book figure attached: diagrammatic presentation of a standard ECG.

**Explanation:** each peak is identified with a letter from P to T that corresponds to a specific electrical activity of the heart.

1. **P-wave:** electrical excitation (**depolarisation**) of the **atria**, which leads to the contraction of both the atria.
2. **QRS complex:** **depolarisation of the ventricles**, which initiates ventricular contraction. The contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of systole.
3. **T-wave:** return of the ventricles from the excited to the normal state (**repolarisation**). The end of the T-wave marks the end of systole.

Counting the number of QRS complexes in a given time gives the heart beat rate. Since ECGs of different individuals have roughly the same shape for a given lead configuration, any deviation indicates a possible abnormality or disease, so the ECG is of great clinical significance.
groundedIn: §15.3.3; Fig. 15.3 — ECG is a graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart; three leads; P-wave atrial depolarisation, QRS ventricular depolarisation, contraction starts shortly after Q, T-wave ventricular repolarisation, end of T-wave marks end of systole; QRS count gives heart rate; clinical significance
